card.summary: What a frequency scout is for. The dark bands of balanced SSFP repeat every 1 / TR in frequency; where the marked regions fall in that pattern depends on the field, on the error of the frequency adjustment, on the material (oil sits 3.4 ppm below water) and on the repetition time, and how wide a band is depends on the material and on the excitation. The target is a 2D image: the slice profile of the selective pulse adds spins at smaller flip angles, whose signal peaks next to the band, so the band is narrower than the hard-pulse formula says and a band model has to carry the slice profile (a 3D acquisition with a hard pulse costs a multiple of the scan time and shows another band). A low bandwidth gives the least noise and the longest repetition time. The answer, for each of the two images, is the lowest bandwidth at which one phase cycle keeps every region clear of the bands with a margin for frequency drift, or the recognition that no single acquisition can, and then the pair of phase cycles that does. By level: level 1 is a measurement task, level 2 is a measurement task, level 3 is a measurement task (a fixed list of scans with a fixed estimator passes this many points below the reference: -1 at level 1, -0.7 at level 2, -0.3 at level 3; 300 instances per level; 25 points or more make a decision task).

1.hints:
How to do it (this level states the method).
  1. Field. Run a gradient echo of your own with two echoes (spgr, n_echoes 2). The off-resonance of a region in Hz is the
     difference of its two phase read-outs / (2 pi x the echo spacing in seconds). The same image shows how far the
     object reaches along y and along x.
  2. Displacement of a region in the EPI = its off-resonance x echo spacing x phase field of view (Hz x s x mm), along
     the phase-encode axis. `plan` prints the echo spacing of a bandwidth. Find, for each phase-encode axis, the lowest
     bandwidth whose largest displacement stays below the limit; a shorter phase field of view lowers it further.
  3. Wrap. The phase field of view must hold the object along the phase-encode axis with about 6 mm to spare on each
     side: centre it on the object with centre_pe_mm (the object does not lie on the isocentre, and the off-resonance
     field moves its edges by the displacement of step 2).
  4. Ghost. In an EPI the ghost of anything lies half a phase field of view away along the phase-encode axis. Relative
     to its source its size is |tan(phi)|, with phi = 2 pi x bandwidth_hz_per_px x matrix x delay x readout coordinate
     of the source / fov_mm (delay in seconds; the readout runs along x when pe_dir is y and along y when pe_dir is x).
     Measure it once in an EPI of your own at a high bandwidth, where a ghost falls on empty space, and solve for the
     delay. The ghost of a marked region in a candidate protocol is then |sin(phi)| at its readout coordinate.
  5. SNR. Run the best candidate once and read the regions. The noise of one pixel is the mean magnitude of a
     signal-free area / 1.253; it scales as matrix x sqrt(lines x bandwidth / averages) / (fov x phase field of view
     in mm), so measure it on any scan with many signal-free pixels and scale it to the candidate.
  6. Deliver the candidate that meets every limit with the fewest averages: the smallest matrix that meets the pixel
     ceiling, the shortest echo time inside the window.

1.statement:
# Measure the fat fraction of each marked disc
A test object lies in the field of view: a disc of gel with 4 smaller discs, each a uniform mixture of water and fat.
Deliver the proton-density fat fraction of each marked disc, in percent, with `submit`:
    fat fraction = 100 x fat protons / (fat protons + water protons),
the share of the signal that is fat when neither T1 nor T2* weights it.
Regions (circles; centre and radius in mm from the isocentre; each lies inside one disc):
  D1: y 39.5, x -20.66, radius 10
  D2: y -22.32, x -38.59, radius 10
  D3: y -41.36, x 16.63, radius 10
  D4: y 11.69, x 43.02, radius 10
The fat fractions lie between 5 and 45 percent.
The fat of this scanner has six peaks (frequency relative to water, share of the fat signal):
    -3.80 ppm 8.7 %, -3.40 ppm 69.4 %, -2.60 ppm 12.8 %, -1.94 ppm 0.4 %, -0.39 ppm 3.9 %, +0.60 ppm 4.8 %
At 1.5 T, 1 ppm is 63.87 Hz. The field at a disc is off resonance by an unknown amount below 80 Hz.
T1 and T2* of the water and of the fat differ from disc to disc and are not known.

Passing: for every disc the delivered fat fraction lies within 3 percentage points of the true one.
The scanner's log must show that you measured. An answer in the wrong unit is wrong.

How to do it (this level states the method; fat is the smaller part of every disc).
  1. Run one `spgr` scan: flip_deg 3, tr_ms 60, n_echoes 6, te_ms 2.3, echo_spacing_ms 2.3, matrix 64,
     partial_fourier 0.75, bandwidth_hz_per_px 800, averages 8. Fat is opposed to water in echoes 1, 3, 5 and
     in phase in echoes 2, 4, 6. (The low flip angle keeps T1 out: at a high one fat, which recovers faster, is over-weighted.)
  2. Read `mean_magnitude` of each disc: m1 ... m6 at the echo times t1 ... t6 (ms). The fat vector of the six peaks is
     c1 = -0.793 at t1, c2 = +0.817 at t2 and c4 = +0.556 at t4 (not -1, +1, +1).
  3. Decay rate from two in-phase echoes, first guess: R = ln(m2 / m4) / (t4 - t2).
  4. The in-phase signal carried back to the first echo time: I = m2 x exp(R x (t2 - t1)).
     F = (I - m1) / (c2 - c1), W = I - c2 x F.
  5. The fat vector shrinks between t2 and t4; take that out of the decay:
     R = ln(m2 x (W + c4 x F) / (m4 x (W + c2 x F))) / (t4 - t2). Do step 4 again with this R.
  6. Fat fraction = 100 x F / (W + F) percent.

1.hints:
How to do it (this level states the method).
  1. Run the target scan at tr_ms 300 twice, with pe_dir y and with pe_dir x. With pe_dir y the ghosts of a tube lie in
     its column, with pe_dir x in its row: what differs between the two images along those lines is the ghosts. A ghost
     can be brighter or darker than the gel under it; the phase image shows it as well.
  2. Read the distance g from the centre of a tube to the centre of its ghost. The law is
     g = (phase field of view) x dist(rate x TR x averages), dist(u) = distance of u from the nearest whole number.
     Here g = 240 mm x rate x 0.3 s, so rate = g / (72 mm s).
  3. A ghost is a copy of the tube. It is off a region whose centre lies D mm from the tube once g is at least
     D + 15 mm, that is from tr = (D + 15 mm) / (240 mm x rate) on.
  4. Take the region that is nearer to the tube and encode the phase along the line that joins it to the tube (pe_dir y
     for region A, x for region B). Deliver that tr plus 5 %.
1.statement:
# The fastest scan that keeps each tube's ghost off its regions
A disc of gel holds three thin tubes of fluid whose signal can pulsate, each at a rate of its own. In an image a
pulsating tube leaves displaced copies of itself (ghosts) along the phase-encode axis; how far they lie from the tube
depends on the timing of the scan.
Each tube has two marked regions: A in its column (same x) and B in its row (same y).
For each tube the examination needs a spin-echo scan of its own, as fast as possible, in which both regions of that
tube are free of its ghost:
    sequence se, te_ms 15, fov_mm 240, matrix 128, bandwidth_hz_per_px 300, 1 average, slice 5 mm;
    you choose pe_dir and tr_ms, with tr_ms from 300 to 1000.
Every tube pulsates, at a few tenths of a hertz. At tr_ms 300 a ghost of every tube lies on one of its regions,
whichever phase-encode axis is chosen.
Tubes (radius 5 mm) and regions (circles of radius 12 mm); positions in mm from the isocentre:
  T1: tube at y -55.6, x -53.6; region T1A at y -28.3, x -53.6; region T1B at y -55.6, x -33.2
  T2: tube at y 1.1, x -1.1; region T2A at y 29.3, x -1.1; region T2B at y 1.1, x 20.8
  T3: tube at y 53.9, x 54.4; region T3A at y 25.8, x 54.4; region T3B at y 53.9, x 32.7
Deliver the two settings of every tube's scan with `submit`. The target scans are not run in this episode: the scanner
evaluates the settings you deliver, without noise.
Your own scans may use any sequence and any parameters the console accepts; only the deliverable is evaluated, on the scan the task names.
That scan is not charged to the scan-time budget and not limited by it.
The rates are not known in advance.

# Phantom QA: measure, judge and diagnose
The scanner is a 3 T system. The uniform section (slice 7) of the ACR large
phantom lies at the isocentre: a disc of solution, 190 mm inner diameter. The scanner may have a fault, two, or none.

1. Run the site's ACR T1 scan and measure on its image:
    sequence se, tr_ms 500, te_ms 20, fov_mm 250, matrix 256, slice_mm 5, averages 1,
    bandwidth_hz_per_px 130, pe_dir x (phase encoding along x, readout along y).
  diameter_y_mm, diameter_x_mm   edge to edge through the centre of the phantom along y, edges at half the mean signal of the 200 cm^2 circle (radius 79.8 mm) centred on the isocentre; the same along x
  piu_percent                    100 (1 - (high - low) / (high + low)): highest and lowest mean of a 1 cm^2 circle (radius 5.64 mm) lying entirely inside the 200 cm^2 circle (radius 79.8 mm) centred on the phantom
  ghosting_ratio                 |((top + bottom) - (left + right)) / (2 large)|: large = mean of the 200 cm^2 circle; the others = mean of 16 x 63 mm rectangles in the background, centred 110 mm from the isocentre, the 63 mm side tangential (top, bottom: along x; left, right: along y)
  (profile gives the numbers along a line, and with samples = 1 the mean of a rectangle; read_regions the mean of circles.)
2. Judge the tests of the ACR guidance:
  geometric_accuracy     fails when a diameter is outside 190 +- 3 mm
  intensity_uniformity   fails when piu_percent is below 80
  ghosting               fails when ghosting_ratio is above 0.03
3. Name every fault of the system. The closed list (a fault moves the test named in brackets):
  gradient_x         [geometric_accuracy] the X gradient (left-right, image columns) is miscalibrated: lengths along x are wrong by the same percentage in every protocol
  gradient_y         [geometric_accuracy] the Y gradient (anterior-posterior, image rows) is miscalibrated: lengths along y are wrong by the same percentage in every protocol
  shim               [geometric_accuracy] the shim left a linear B0 gradient across the phantom: the image is stretched or compressed along the readout axis, in proportion to 1 / bandwidth
  b1_transmit        [intensity_uniformity] the transmit field is too high or too low near the centre of the phantom (the flip angle is off there)
  receive_coil       [intensity_uniformity] a receive coil element is down: the receive sensitivity falls off across the phantom
  signal_instability [ghosting] the signal amplitude varies from pulse to pulse (transmitter, receiver or gradient amplifier)
  phantom_motion     [ghosting] the phantom is not fixed: it rocks along the phase-encode axis during the scan
  A failed test is not a diagnosis: more than one fault moves each test. A failed test has exactly one fault. The
  scan-time budget leaves room after the QA scan for a short scan of your own design that tells them apart. A fault
  in the list is either present (its test fails) or absent; small imperfections that fail no test are not faults.

1.hints:
How to do it (this level states the method).
  1. Take one localiser that shows the whole object with a pixel of 1 mm: `spgr` with tr_ms 11, flip_deg 20,
     fov_mm 256, matrix 256, averages 2. It takes 12.6 s: the budget pays one such scan.
  2. Edges of the object with `profile`: a profile along y through the isocentre (position_mm 0, width_mm 20). Take
     low and high where it first and last crosses half of the level of the gel; the same along x (the dark inserts
     lie on that line: only the outermost crossings count).
  3. Spacing of a pair: `profile` along x through the centre of its region (position_mm = the region's y, width_mm 4,
     from the region's x - 11 to x + 11). It shows two peaks. Let h be half of the highest value. The samples above
     h form two groups; the position of a group is the mean of its positions weighted with (value - h).
     Spacing S = the difference of the two positions.
  4. Pixel P = 0.55 x S (a pixel as large as the spacing merges the two; 0.55 x S gives a dip of at least 0.5).
  5. Phase-encode along y, the short side: pe_dir y. The image reaches from -FOV / 2 - P / 2 to FOV / 2 - P / 2 about the
     isocentre, so along each axis half = max(-low - P / 2, high + P / 2) + 2 mm.
     lines = 2 x ceil(half_y / P), matrix = max(2 x ceil(half_x / P), lines, 32), fov_mm = P x matrix,
     phase_fov = lines / matrix.

A region read-out is a mean over the image as reconstructed: with partial Fourier the image takes its phase from a

Passing: for every region the delivered T1 lies within a factor 1.1 of the true T1 (between T1 / 1.1 and 1.1 x T1).
The scanner's log must show that you measured. An answer in the wrong unit is wrong.

How to do it (this level states the procedure).
  1. Run three inversion-recovery scans: sequence ir, tr_ms 1500, matrix 32 (no partial Fourier), with
     ti_ms 30, 400 and 1450. Each costs 52.5 s. Read out the marked regions.
  2. Sign the read-outs. At ti_ms 1450 every material is past its null, so its signal is positive: S3 =
     `complex_mean_magnitude`. A read-out of the same region whose `complex_mean_phase_rad` differs from that of the
     ti_ms 1450 scan by more than pi / 2 (after wrapping the difference into -pi .. pi) is negative: S = -magnitude.
  3. At a fixed repetition time the signal is exactly S(TI) = a - b exp(-TI / T1). a and b drop out of
         q = (S3 - S2) / (S2 - S1) = (exp(-400 / T1) - exp(-1450 / T1)) / (exp(-30 / T1) - exp(-400 / T1)).
     The right side grows with T1. Find the T1 at which it equals the measured q, by bisection between 50 and 5000 ms.
  4. Deliver that T1 in milliseconds for the region.
Do not use S = M (1 - 2 exp(-TI / T1)): it assumes a repetition time of many T1 and a complete inversion.
